record.paper_title: Recent advances in open billiards with some open problems
record.original_question: In mushroom billiards and similar mixed-phase-space billiards, how can one characterize escape at the boundary between regular and chaotic regions, including the possible slowing of survival decay by sticky marginally unstable periodic orbits and by the regular-chaotic boundary itself when the hole lies in the chaotic region?

evidence.quote: The decay of the survival probability in the case that the hole is in the chaotic region may be significantly slowed both by stickiness due to marginally unstable periodic orbits, and by the boundary itself.
Open problem 11. Characterise the escape properties of the boundary between regular and chaotic regions in mushroom and similar billiards.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider a mushroom billiard: a planar domain consisting of a semicircular "cap" attached to a rectangular "stem", in which a point particle moves in straight lines and reflects elastically off the boundary. The phase space of this dynamical system is mixed: it contains an invariant regular region (corresponding to trajectories that remain in the cap forever, integrable in nature) and an invariant chaotic region; these two regions are separated by a sharp boundary in phase space. The chaotic region typically contains families of marginally unstable periodic orbits (MUPOs), namely periodic orbits with neutral linear stability that occupy zero volume in phase space but cause intermittent "sticky" dynamics, and a single MUPO family is known to contribute a term proportional to 1/t to the survival probability.

Now make the billiard "open" by removing a small arc (a "hole") from the boundary, located in the chaotic component. Let P(t) denote the survival probability, i.e. the measure (with respect to a natural invariant measure on the chaotic component, e.g. the Liouville measure conditioned on the chaotic region) of initial conditions whose forward trajectory has not yet hit the hole by time t.

Problem. Characterize the escape dynamics associated with the boundary between the regular and chaotic regions in mushroom billiards (and analogous mixed-phase-space billiards). In particular:

(a) Quantify how the asymptotic decay of P(t) as t → ∞ is influenced by the family of marginally unstable periodic orbits embedded in the chaotic component.
(b) Quantify the additional contribution to slowing of the decay coming from the regular–chaotic boundary itself, independently of the MUPO contribution.
(c) Provide asymptotic formulas (with explicit constants depending on the geometry of the mushroom, the position and size of the hole, and the invariant measure) for P(t) that simultaneously account for both effects.
artifact.status_search_result: Partial results exist: it is known that a single MUPO family contributes a C/t term to the survival probability in mushroom billiards, and stickiness near the regular-chaotic boundary has been studied numerically and heuristically (e.g., "How sticky is the chaos/order boundary?" and related works on intermittent billiards). However, a complete characterization of escape at the regular–chaotic boundary, including a rigorous asymptotic for P(t) that combines MUPO stickiness with boundary stickiness, does not appear to have been obtained, so the problem remains open in its general form.

status_evidence.title: How sticky is the chaos/order boundary?
status_evidence.snippet: Stickiness investigated as the probability of remaining in the mushroom cap for at least time t given uniform initial conditions in the chaotic part.
status_evidence.claim: The regular-chaotic boundary stickiness has been studied but no complete asymptotic formula is established.

status_evidence.title: Escape from Intermittent Billiards (Georgiou thesis)
status_evidence.snippet: A MUPO leads to a contribution to P(t) proportional to 1/t as t →∞.
status_evidence.claim: MUPO contribution to survival decay is partially characterized.

status_evidence.title: Survival Probability for the Stadium Billiard
status_evidence.snippet: Almost all mushroom configurations give rise to families of marginally unstable periodic orbits where P(t) ∼ C/t.
status_evidence.claim: The 1/t MUPO contribution is known; separating boundary contribution is not.
